# Preface

...the **history of heretics** has been presented in all its particulars, even the smallest details; I do not believe the accounts of religious errors and heresies in those large volumes appear at all the same as they were initially drafted in this small book.

I felt it necessary to mention this here as a reminder, so that no one assumes they will find in the present work merely a brief extract of what is more extensively detailed in those two <term>folio volumes</term> <note>Large, prestigious books printed on full-sized sheets of paper; the author refers here to his massive two-volume *Impartial History of the Church and Heretics*.</note>. Rather, this book is primarily composed for those who desire a general and summary understanding of all church affairs, especially for students who love such knowledge, and most of all for the youth. The history of heretics, however, encompasses countless other subjects and assumes <note>original Latin: "præsupponiret"</note> that the reader already possesses some chronological understanding <note>original Latin: "connexion"</note> of historical eras and events in their proper sequence.

Moreover, one finds here a sufficient, thorough, and clear introduction to the history of the Old Testament, which is not to be found elsewhere. Thus, one can easily see once more that both books belong almost inseparably together, and that each may suitably compensate for the other’s omissions.

# Preface

And this is precisely why I have not wished to undertake any expansion or continuation of the present *edition*. A discerning reader can find more than enough information in the large book; however, providing a *continuation* up until the end of this *century* <note>original Latin: "seculi"</note> would give me pause for the reasons I cited in the third part of the **History of Heretics** <note>A reference to his massive work, the *Impartial History of the Church and Heretics* (1699), which revolutionized the field by treating "heretics" with sympathy.</note>.

My wish in this regard is that God would awaken many sincere souls and make them capable of investigating these necessary and important matters in a truly thorough and <term>impartial</term> <note>The concept of being "impartial" (*unparteyiſch*) was the author's core philosophy; it meant looking for Christian truth outside of official church dogmas and being fair to those labeled as "heretics."</note> manner, and also to uncover even the most recent **church history** wisely and without a misguided love for the parties and sects of this world. Not only will I rejoice at this, but I will also show myself indebted to anyone who sincerely and modestly points out the errors I have made in such a *study* <note>original Latin: "studio"</note> and corrects them for the common good. For such souls, and no others, are fit to perform this kind of work, which will hopefully prove all the more important in *practice* <note>original Latin: "praxi"</note> in the future, given how poorly and perversely it has been handled until now by all the religious parties.

> May God increase the power of His light in
> and among us all, to His great glory!

# Preface

...the **history of heretics** was laid out before one's eyes in all, even the most minute circumstances; I need not even mention how the accounts of **religious errors** and **heresies** in those volumes have taken on an entirely different appearance throughout than what was initially drafted in this small book.

This seemed necessary for me to mention here, so that no one might think that he would find in the present writing a mere brief extract of what was only more extensively detailed in those two <term>folio volumes</term> <note>original: "Folianten". Folios were the largest book format of the time, printed on large sheets of paper folded only once, signifying a massive and expensive scholarly work.</note>.

Rather, this book is primarily composed for those who desire a general and summary understanding of all **church affairs**, and especially for students who are enthusiasts of such knowledge, but most of all for the youth. The **history of heretics**, however, extends across countless other subjects and <term>presupposes</term> <note>original Latin-derived: "præsupponiret"</note>, as it were, that the reader already possesses some **chronological connection** <note>original: "chronologische connexion", meaning a basic understanding of how historical events and time periods link together.</note> of periods and stories in their proper order.

Furthermore, one finds here a sufficient, thorough, and clear introduction to the history of the **Old Testament**, which is not to be found elsewhere. For this reason, one can again easily see that both books belong together almost inseparably, and that one can fittingly compensate for the shortcomings of the other.

# Preface

<meta>catchword: Remembrance</meta>

And this is precisely what caused me to refrain from making any expansion or continuation in this present edition. For a discerning reader can find more than enough information in the larger volume; however, providing a continuation up to the end of this <term>century</term> <note>original Latin: "seculi". Here referring to the 17th century, as this was written around the year 1700.</note> seems problematic to me for the reasons I cited in the third part of the **History of Heretics** <note>original: "ketzer-historie". This refers to Arnold's massive and controversial "Unparteyische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie" (Impartial History of the Church and Heretics), which challenged traditional church views.</note>.

My wish here is that God would awaken and equip many sincere minds to investigate these necessary and important matters thoroughly and impartially, and to uncover even the most recent **church history** wisely, without a misguided devotion to the world’s parties and sects. I shall not only rejoice in this but will also show myself indebted to anyone who sincerely and modestly points out the errors I have made in this <term>study</term> <note>original Latin: "studio"</note> and corrects them for the common good. For such minds, and no others, are fit to perform this kind of work, which will hopefully prove all the more important in <term>practice</term> <note>original Latin: "praxi"</note> in the future, given how poorly and perversely it has been handled by all the various **religious parties** until now.

May God increase the power of His light within and among us all, to His great glory!

# Remembrance to the Reader.

->Kind Reader!<-

This history comes to light, so to speak, in a small stature <note>original: "kleinen statur". This refers to the physical format of the book—likely a smaller, cheaper octavo or duodecimo—meant to be more affordable and portable than a massive scholarly folio.</note>, and speaks only our common **mother tongue** <note>original: "muttersprache". At the turn of the 18th century, most academic and "serious" histories were still written in Latin. Writing in German was a deliberate choice to reach the layperson and the working class.</note>. Both of these factors assure us immediately that it was not composed for great and learned people. And this is indeed true in itself, as the author recently allowed himself to be persuaded by several individuals to draft a brief, clear summary for young people and others who cannot inform themselves <note>original: "erholen", which in this context means to derive knowledge or recover information.</note> from Latin books. Therefore, the sensible reader will not expect a grand affair from such a small work.

For one can hardly promise him more here than an **impartial investigation** <term>unpartheyische untersuchung</term> <note>This was the author's scholarly trademark: attempting to look at history without the bias of established church denominations.</note> of historical events, faithful accounts thereof, as well as a thorough connection of the same, and the brevity preferred therein. Neither the short amount of time nor the available space permitted anything more on this occasion. In his method, the author has followed his purpose, which is to present a sufficient understanding of the primary matters alongside the circumstances of time, persons, place, and so forth.

<note>The following key terms were highlighted for the reader: Remembrance to the Reader, Mother tongue, History, Impartial investigation, Method.</note>

### Remembrance to the Reader.

He has compiled the subject matters that a diligent mind seeks to find together. And from this has come the division of every **century** <note>original: "seculi", the Latin genitive for century.</note> into five main parts. Into which, in my opinion, everything flows that is necessary to know about them. For any change in this regard would have confused young and simple <note>original: "einfältigen". In this context, it refers to "plain" or "ordinary" readers without specialized academic training, rather than a lack of intelligence.</note> readers, especially since no **detailed explanation** <note>original: "deduction", referring to a formal, logical derivation or a lengthy scholarly proof.</note> was added, as such would have taken up too much space.

On the other hand, out of a desire to learn the truth, the author has not always been able to follow others in the matters themselves. Common law has granted him the freedom to do so, which everyone may enjoy in a **question of fact** <term>quæstione facti: a legal and philosophical term referring to the determination of what actually happened, as opposed to how the law or church doctrine should be applied to those events.</term>. Specifically, when the question concerns a certain history, insofar as it rests upon this or that person and either accuses or acquits them. For a **historian** <term>historicus</term> generally goes only this far with his narrative, leaving the **application** <term>application: the moral or practical conclusion drawn from historical facts.</term> to others, who may then decide whether or not to turn it into a general rule.

And certainly, if **church history** <note>original: "kirchen-historie"</note> were generally pursued without so many harmful prejudices, one would soon be amazed at its usefulness. I will give only one example here. In the history of the **heretics** <note>original: "ketzer". The author, Gottfried Arnold, was famous for arguing that those labeled "heretics" were often the true Christians.</note> who, by the **Papists** <note>original: "Papisten", a term used by Protestant writers of this era to refer to Roman Catholics, often implying they followed the Pope rather than the Bible.</note> before **Luther** <note>The text ends mid-sentence, leading into the name of the reformer Martin Luther.</note>

<summary>The author explains the book's division into five parts per century and defends his right as a historian to investigate "questions of fact" independently of tradition. He argues that church history is most useful when studied without prejudice, particularly regarding those labeled as heretics.</summary>

...Luther were made to do so, most even among the Protestant writers <note>original: "scribenten", referring to professional writers or chroniclers.</note> took the horrific accusations from the Papist reports <note>original: "Papistischen relationen"; the author is referring to Roman Catholic accounts of history.</note>. However, if one were to assume from constant practice that those gentlemen have always wronged the witnesses of truth and never reported straightforwardly, then very strange histories would often emerge that would run completely contrary to current common reports.

In the histories of the conversion of the heathens <note>original: "Heyden", meaning non-Christians or pagans.</note> and other similar points, the same would also prove true, if one did not unthinkingly take everything from biased reporters. I must confess that I have often been startled when I saw how generally the best people under the Papacy were subjected to such heavy accusations, and indeed by such authors who intend to uphold a common cause against the Papacy. How thoroughly, however, could the innocence of many be saved and malice be put to shame if one proceeded impartially <note>original: "unpartheyisch", a key term for the author, Gottfried Arnold, who was famous for his "Impartial History of the Church and Heretics."</note> in this? Suffice it to say that our church history <note>original: "Kirchen-historie"</note> has reached its full degree of perfection as little as other branches of learning <term>erudition: refers to scholarly knowledge and the formal academic study of history.</term>, nor does it stand in its proper use.

### Remembrance to the Reader.

<meta>catchword: For</meta>

In the future, many will encounter these and other histories who might wish to provide a more detailed report on various points. He <note>The author, Gottfried Arnold, refers to himself in the third person here.</note> will also likely not excuse himself at all, nor resist for long through much disputation; rather, he will grasp with both hands whatever is suggested from honest intentions and based on truth, without mockery or a desire for blame. For in such a case, he commits himself only to accepting the reminders of others. To other bickering <note>original: "gezäncke"</note>, he will contribute nothing, as before, and will not increase the number of polemical writings <term>polemical writings: "Streit-Schrifften," refers to pamphlets or books written specifically for theological debate or controversy.</term> by even a single page. There are, in any case, already other means to defend the truth.

To anyone else who perhaps does not like the reports on the origin of certain church customs <note>original: "kirchen-gebräuche"</note> or other stories, his opinion remains unoffended. Especially since brevity has forbidden presenting more reasons. For this brevity was so strongly recommended to the author <note>original: "autori"</note> that he could neither include any citations from authors <note>original: "locum der autorum," referring to specific passages or source citations</note> nor carry out the final chapters of the last two centuries <note>original: "seculis"</note> exactly as desired. Therefore, he has had to postpone everything for another occasion, as these and other such things are well in need of further investigation.

### Notice to the Reader.

In the future, many will come across these and other histories who might wish to provide a more precise report on this or that point. The author will presumably not make excuses or defend himself at length through much disputing <term>disputing: original "disputirens," referring to the formal, often aggressive academic debates common in 17th-century theology</term>; rather, he will embrace with both hands whatever is suggested with honest intentions and based on the ground of truth, without mockery or a spirit of fault-finding. For in such a case, he considers himself duty-bound only to accept the suggestions of others. To any other quarreling he will, as he has done until now, contribute nothing, and he will not increase the number of polemical writings <term>polemical writings: original "Streit-Schrifften," printed pamphlets or books written specifically to attack the theological positions of others</term> by even a single page. There are other means anyway to uphold the truth.

Furthermore, if anyone happens to be displeased by the reports on the origin of certain church customs <note>Arnold often argued that many "sacred" church traditions were actually later human inventions rather than divine mandates.</note> or other histories, their own opinion remains unoffended. This is especially so since brevity has prevented the laying out of further evidence. For this brevity was so strongly recommended to the author that he could neither include citations from the authorities <note>original: "locum der autorum," referring to specific passages or proof-texts from historical and theological authors.</note> nor execute the final chapters of the last two centuries <note>original: "seculis," Latin for centuries.</note> as properly as he wished. Therefore, he has had to postpone everything to another occasion, as these and other such matters certainly require further investigation.

<summary>The author invites constructive, truth-based criticism while refusing to engage in the bitter theological polemics of his day. He also notes that the work's brevity—enforced by external recommendations—limited his ability to provide full citations or detailed coverage of recent centuries.</summary>

### Notice to the Reader.

For just as there has been a lack of many necessary books in our language <note>The author refers to German, which at this time was often passed over for Latin in serious academic or theological writing.</note> until now, despite their infinite quantity, so it is no less the case with such works as this. And since so much useless, irritating, and irresponsible material in the German language has been presented even to the most innocent minds, one can hardly find even a small church history <term>church history: original "kirchen-historie," the study of the development of the Christian church</term> in the hands of the unlearned. Indeed, something of this sort has recently been attempted with the translated *Gotha Church History* <note>original: "Gothischen kirchen-historie," likely referring to the influential *Compendium Historiae Ecclesiasticae* commissioned by Duke Ernst the Pious of Saxe-Gotha to educate the laity.</note>. It has already been of great use among the learned with its Latin edition <note>original: "lateinischen edition"</note> and maintains its great value. But whether it achieves its purpose among young and simple people, one must let others judge.

Now, while we are even less inclined to present the current book as perfect and would gladly wait for better work from others, yet one can assure this one thing: that the author was moved by good friends to look solely to the capacity of youth <term>capacity of youth: original Latin "captum der jugend," referring to the intellectual reach or level of understanding of young people</term> and others. Or to put it briefly, he had to write in German and clearly for Germans. Had one wanted to translate another Latin history immediately, perhaps none would have achieved the purpose. Although they certainly all do their part, except that

### Notice to the Reader.

<meta>The first word "genheit" is the completion of "gelegenheit" (opportunity) from the previous page's catchword.</meta>is the one who has it best, who can compare <note>original: "conferiren," from the Latin *conferre*.</note> them all with one another and make use of the best from them. But this is possible for very few.

The diligent investigation of the church histories <term>church histories: accounts of the development and struggles of the Christian faith</term> published until now shows that very few are suitable for unlearned and simple minds. I will not even speak of the universal histories <term>universal histories: historical works that attempt to cover the entire human story, mixing secular and religious events</term>, which mix worldly and church history together and thereby give the reader a somewhat confused concept of the matters from the start.

Among the church histories that have become known among Protestants <note>original: "Protestirenden"</note> since the Reformation, the *Magdeburg Centuries* <note>original: "Magdeburgischen centuriæ," a massive 13-volume work from the 16th century intended to prove the Lutheran church was the true heir to the early church.</note> are too large and extensive for such people, and perhaps also the *Epitome of Osiander* <note>original: "epitome Osiandri," a condensed summary of church history by the theologian Lucas Osiander.</note>, a part of which David Förter translated into German.

The smaller authors who followed have also done their part, but nevertheless have not always satisfied every reader. For in the previous century <note>The 1600s.</note>, many still lacked sufficient information. Their intention also rarely goes further than the exposure of the Papacy <note>original: "entdeckung des Pabstthums," referring to the common Protestant goal of highlighting perceived errors or corruption in the Roman Catholic Church.</note>. Some only began to more closely investigate the old controversies <note>original: "controversien," formal theological disputes.</note> for the sake of their own party, which were perhaps being stirred up again. And many a person indeed has the will, but not the opportunity

...opportunity and freedom to write something impartial. Very few in this century <note>original: "seculo"</note> have come through the vast sea all the way to the shore and brought their history <note>original: "historie"</note> to a conclusion.

Therefore, no one is easily to be blamed if they do not hit the mark exactly here and there. Considering that this study <term>study: from the Latin *studium*, referring to a dedicated branch of learning or academic pursuit</term> is so very extensive and obscure that it often gives even the most skillful mind much to puzzle over, and requires a truly free and experienced person to handle it. For this reason, a sensible reader will also use the proper approach with this book. If anyone is inclined to point out a correction <note>In this context, the author is inviting scholarly critique or "reminders" of facts he may have missed.</note>, let them be so kind as to send their reasons <note>original: "rationes," meaning the logical arguments or evidence for a correction.</note> to the publisher <term>publisher: the *verleger*, the person responsible for the printing and distribution of the work</term>. In doing so, they may live assured that in the next edition <note>original: "edition"</note>, they shall be fully satisfied in accordance with fairness. Likewise, if any other uncommon observations <note>original: "observationibus," referring to noteworthy historical details or scholarly findings</note> regarding this matter were at hand, the reader is requested to be inclined to share <note>original: "communiciren," meaning to communicate or provide information</note> them.

# The History of the Church
### of the Old Testament.

## Preparation.

The entire history of the Old Testament can be conveniently divided into seven epochs <term>epochs: major historical periods or stages marked by significant events</term> or parts, the order of which may be as follows, following almost exactly the guidance found in Matthew, chapter 1, verse 17 <note>In the Gospel of Matthew, the genealogy of Jesus is divided into three sets of fourteen generations; the author here expands this biblical structure into seven historical periods.</note>.

I. From the creation of the world until the Great Flood <note>original: *sündfluth*</note>.
II. From the Great Flood until Abraham's departure <note>The "departure" refers to Abraham leaving his homeland for the Land of Canaan as commanded by God.</note>.
III. From Abraham's departure until the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt.
IV. From the departure of the children of Israel until the time of their Kings.
V. From the beginning of the Kings until the Babylonian captivity <note>original: *gefängniß*, literally meaning imprisonment or bondage, referring to the forced detention of Jews in Babylon.</note>.
VI. From the Babylonian captivity until the Maccabees <note>The Maccabees were Jewish leaders who led a rebellion against the Seleucid Empire in the 2nd century BCE.</note>.
VII. From the Maccabees until Jesus Christ.

# Preparation.

In each part or period <term>period: a specific stage or division of history</term>, we intend first and foremost to look to the true order of those persons and things which are found in the Bible, and specifically according to their most significant circumstances that might serve to explain divine works and prophecies. Alongside this, the synchronisms <term>synchronisms: events occurring at the same time in different parts of the world</term> of other well-known matters shall be included, which occurred elsewhere in the world at that same time. Everything, however, shall be proven by citing scriptural passages and by drawing from the most reliable Jewish, Christian, and pagan writers <note>original: *scribenten*</note>, especially Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus was a first-century Jewish historian whose works provide crucial context for biblical history</note>, as well as the Church Fathers <note>original: *patribus*; the influential early Christian teachers and bishops</note>, historians, and chronologists. And since these few pages are intended to draft a brief church history, the focus will primarily be on the state of the true Church in contrast to the false one. For this reason, the circumstances of the creation <note>original: *schöpffung*</note> have been skipped at the very beginning, as they can otherwise be easily and independently taken from Moses <note>The author refers to the Pentateuch, the first five books of the Bible traditionally attributed to Moses</note>. Regarding the biblical books and their authors, it was found necessary to say a bit more, because such information is not easily found in our language <note>The author is writing in German, noting that scholarly biblical criticism was often only available in Latin at this time</note> or in such a concise form.

Mos.*; the author refers to the Pentateuch, though the plagues are specifically found in the Second Book of Moses, or Exodus</note> chapters 3 to 12). *Josephus* <note>Flavius Josephus was a famous 1st-century Jewish historian whose "Antiquities of the Jews" was a primary source for early modern history writers.</note>.
<margin>10 plagues.</margin>

<margin>Passover.</margin>
§. 2. On the evening before the night of the departure on the 14th of April (which month was called Abib or Nisan <note>The Hebrew months of the ecclesiastical and civil calendars, respectively.</note>), they ate the Passover (chapter 12) after they and their ancestors had been strangers for 430 years (verses 40, 42). However, they did not take the direct path toward the promised land, otherwise they would have arrived soon; rather, they had to turn toward the Red Sea and toward the Arabian deserts so that God might test them, specifically for forty years.

<margin>Miracles.</margin>
§. 3. The miracles involved therein were primarily the dividing and drying of the sea (chapter 14:16ff.), the pillars of cloud and fire, Pharaoh’s destruction (chapter 16:23 <note>This likely refers to the completion of the crossing or a citation for the song of praise in the following chapters.</note>), the sweetening of the water at Marah (chapter 15:2), the feeding by quails (chapter 16:13) and manna (chapter 16:15), the water from the rock (chapter 17:6), the victory against the Amalekites, and so forth. *Josephus*.

<margin>The Law.</margin>
§. 4. Upon Mount Sinai, God gives the law (The Second Book of Moses <note>Exodus</note> 19:24). This was followed by the ceremonial and political laws (chapter 20 and following). *Josephus*.

### Chapter IV.
## From the Babylonian Captivity to the Maccabees.

->§. 1.<-

<margin>Time of the Babylonian captivity. 8. 20.</margin>The Babylonian captivity lasted 70 years, according to 2 Chronicles 36, Jeremiah 25 and 29, and Daniel 9:2. This duration is calculated either from the fourth year of King Jehoiakim according to Daniel 9:1, or from the deportation of Jeconiah and the 18,000 people according to Ezekiel 1 and 38 <note>The reference to Ezekiel 38 may be a scribal error for a different chapter, such as 33 or 40, which deal with the fall of the city.</note>, or even from the total destruction of the city and the temple. <margin>3349</margin>Among these, the second chronological calculation is the most common and begins from the year of the world 3349 <term>year of the world</term><note>original: "jahr der welt"; also known as Anno Mundi (AM), a calendar era based on the biblical creation of the world.</note>.

<margin>Condition of the people.</margin>§. 2. During the captivity itself, the people did not improve; instead, they mostly grew worse through the temptation of idolatry, as the prophets lament in Ezekiel 20, 21, 23, and 36. Their descendants later acknowledged and repented for this, as seen in Nehemiah 9 and 10, Ezra 9, and Daniel 9.

<margin>Books of the Chronicles.</margin>

The Herodians, or servants of Herod, *Matthew 22:16, Mark 12:13,* were so named after Herod the Great, and were either people who took Herod to be the Christ, or otherwise mixed pagan customs with Judaism. At the very least, nothing certain is known of them. Perhaps they were Herod's flatterers, as *Tertullian* and *Epiphanius* believe.

§. 28. Among these sects, the Pharisees were the most popular of all because of their pretense and hypocrisy. The others, because they were more inclined toward a serious, quiet nature, were not as highly regarded. They all lasted together, however, until Judaism itself came to an end <note>The author refers here to the end of the Jewish commonwealth and the destruction of the Temple in 70 CE.</note>.

During this, 97,000 Jews were taken prisoner,

The history of the New Testament can most conveniently be divided into 17 <term>secula<gloss>centuries or hundred-year periods</gloss></term>. We intend to organize each century into several chapters so that we may briefly outline:

I. The external state of Christendom, from which one can immediately see the internal condition of the Christians. Since they were mostly in persecutions

<margin>Anointing at Bethany. Triumphal Entry.</margin>

<margin>Greeks. Voice from heaven.</margin>
The Greeks wish to see Jesus, who then teaches them and is confirmed by the voice from heaven, John 12:20-50, Mark 11:11.

<margin>Fig tree. Merchants in the temple.</margin>
§. 55. The following morning, or four days before Easter <note>original: "ostern." In this historical context, the author uses the German word for Easter to refer to the Jewish Passover.</note>, he goes again toward Jerusalem, curses the fig tree, drives the merchants <note>Often referred to as the money-changers.</note> out of the temple; in the evening he returns to Bethany. The next day he enters the city again and finds the fig tree withered, Mark 11:12-26, Matt. 21:12-22, Luke 19:45-48.

<margin>Baptism of John. Vinedressers. King's wedding.</margin>
§. 56. Here he enters Jerusalem again, speaks there of the baptism of John and of the wicked vinedressers <term>vinedressers<gloss>A parable describing tenants of a vineyard who refuse to give the owner his share and eventually kill his son.</gloss></term>, as well as of the King’s wedding feast, Matt. 21:23-46, ch. 22:1-14, Mark 11:27-33, ch. 12:1-12, Luke 20:1-20.

<margin>Tribute money. Greatest commandment. Woe to the Pharisees.</margin>

Here, the testimony of Pliny <note>Pliny the Younger (c. 61–113 AD), a Roman governor whose letters provide some of the earliest non-Christian accounts of the movement.</note>, a pagan, shall be enough for us, who writes of them thus: <margin>Testimony of the enemies.</margin> "They bind themselves to one another in their assemblies, not for malice, but so that they will commit no murder, adultery, or theft; that they do no wrong to anyone, nor withhold what belongs to another, etc. Moreover, even through torture, nothing incriminating could be forced out of two female persons <note>Pliny’s letter mentions questioning two female slaves called "deaconesses" to understand Christian rituals.</note>."

§. 3. Those who wrote the apologies <note>From the Greek "apologia," meaning a formal legal defense; these were open letters written to Emperors to explain and defend Christian practices.</note> also appealed boldly before the authorities and the whole world to the innocent and holy lives of the Christians. They offered themselves up to any punishment if even a single Christian could be convicted of a crime. Regarding their private life, they confessed that they did nothing, besides their work, but sing, pray, and contemplate divine things. They were also not ashamed to say that even the women discussed God's word while at the spinning wheel. *Justin, Athenagoras, Tatian, Theophilus of Antioch.*

<margin>Separation from the Pagans.</margin>
§. 4. The constant uncertainty they faced among their enemies also taught them to heed the Word all the more eagerly, and it prevented all complacency and lukewarmness. They also separated themselves from all other pagan abominations, such as stage plays <note>original: "schauspielen"; this refers to the Roman theater and gladiatorial games, which early Christians avoided due to their perceived immorality and connection to idol worship.</note>,

§. 15. Their fasting was indeed without compulsion, yet earnest and full of good intentions, especially among new converts. Tertullian also turned to this party, and indeed, as historians admit, out of a love for a serious and disciplined life, and likewise because the Roman clergy persecuted him greatly out of envy. But only because they teach that one must fast more often and live more moderately than one should marry and use the marriage bed. ### Concerning Errors and Heresies.

<margin>Jesus Christ.</margin>
<margin>Alogi.</margin>
<margin>Theodotus.</margin>
§. 31. The Alogi <note>A name given by Epiphanius to a group that rejected the Gospel of John and the Book of Revelation, derived from the Greek meaning "without the Word" or "unreasonable."</note> are said to have rejected the doctrine of the Word <note>original: $\lambda\acute{o}\gamma\omega$ (logos)</note> or Christ, and consequently the writings of John. Theodotus was the originator of this, who, after his denial of Christ, stated: He had only denied a mere man. *Augustine, Epiphanius, Theodoret.*

<margin>170</margin>
<margin>Hermogenes.</margin>
<margin>Praxeas.</margin>
§. 32. Tertullian wrote a book against Hermogenes because he established a primeval matter that would have been eternal alongside God. Likewise against Praxeas, who held Christ to be God the Father Himself, and taught that the Father had also been crucified <note>This theological position is known as Patripassianism, from the Latin words for "Father" and "suffering."</note>.

<margin>Dispute regarding the Easter festival.</margin>
§. 33. Otherwise, at the end of this century, a great disruption occurred with the dispute over the timing of the Easter festival. For since this had once been adopted from Judaism, most celebrated it at the same time as the Jews, namely on the 14th day of the Easter month <note>The month of Nisan in the Hebrew calendar; those who followed this practice were called Quartodecimans.</note>. Others always held it on a Sunday, as is still the practice today.

§. 34. Regarding this matter, the earlier Christians certainly allowed one another freedom of practice. But afterward, the Roman Bishop Victor wanted to force all the Asian churches to conform to his practice and even excommunicated them. For this, Irenaeus and others contradicted him, and a great schism arose. From this, the beginning decline of the initial purity among the teachers is already visible. *Irenaeus & Melito in Eusebius.* Just as their doctrine and deeds otherwise no longer agreed in all things with the very first Christians.

<margin>Under Maximinus.</margin>

This happened mostly out of enmity toward Alexander Severus <note>the previous emperor</note>, who had kept an image of Christ in his palace and constantly repeated the words: **Do unto others as you would have them do unto you;** <note>original: "Was du willt, das man dir thun soll, das thue andern auch;" the Golden Rule</note> for he [Alexander] also gladly tolerated the Christians around himself and his mother Mamaea. *Lampridius, Vopiscus, Eusebius, Orosius.*

§. 2. Those who still wished to perform their office faithfully nonetheless occasionally persisted in their own opinions and dogmas, for which they pushed others aside. ### Third Century. Chapter II.

<margin>Ceremonies.</margin>
Now, more formalities and ceremonies, outward holiness, and appearance emerged. All of this hindered souls from a true internal change and led them away from the inward to the outward, making them trust in and rely upon the "work performed" <term>opus operatum</term> <note>original: "opere operato"; a theological concept suggesting that a religious rite is effective simply by being performed, regardless of the spiritual state of the person performing it</note>.

§. 5. Thus, one already reads so much in the teachers of these times about sacrifices, priests, altars, anointings, consecrations, and similar things. They took these figures of speech metaphorically from Judaism and Paganism, until finally the physical practices themselves followed.

<margin>Houses of prayer.</margin>
§. 6. And because there was a long period of outward peace and safety from enemies in this century <note>original: "seculo"; Latin for century or age</note>, they established themselves more firmly in all things. People were already building specific houses in which they gathered regularly. In accordance with superstitious opinions—as if the church consisted of the outward—these were called <term>churches</term> <note>original: "ἐκκλησίας" (ekklēsias); the Greek word for an assembly or congregation</note> or congregations, as well as houses of God, houses of prayer, etc. In reality, however, these were still private buildings, and small and simple at that—not the great palaces, temples, or churches that emerged later. *Eusebius.* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the primary historian of the early Church.</note>

<margin>Other places.</margin>
§. 7. Yet even these did not last long, for Diocletian <note>Roman Emperor (reigned 284–305 AD) who launched the "Great Persecution," the last and most severe imperial attempt to suppress Christianity</note> soon had them torn down. They then gathered again wherever they could, whether it be a hall or a stable, a prison, a tomb, or a cellar. This led to the pagan accusation that Christians, as atheists <note>In antiquity, "atheist" was a term of reproach for those who refused to worship the traditional Roman gods</note>, had no temples. *Eusebius, Minucius Felix, Origen, Clement of Alexandria.*

### III Century. Chapter II.

<margin>Fasting.</margin>...which they also used otherwise. For fasting, certain times were now set aside, especially before Easter, and in the Latin congregations on Saturdays, whereby much gradually grew into superstition. *The same authors.* <note>original: "Iidem Auctor."; referring to the sources cited on the previous page, likely Tertullian and Cyprian.</note>

<margin>Baptism.</margin>§. 12. Baptism was also mixed with many ceremonies, such as giving the candidates honey and milk to taste, anointing them, adorning them with white garments and wreaths, and so forth. (*Tertullian, Cyprian, Author of the Apostolic Constitutions.* <note>The Apostolic Constitutions is a late 4th-century collection of ecclesiastical law, formerly attributed to the apostles.</note>) Regarding the baptism of small children, it was not yet so common or firmly established. Therefore, Tertullian always advised that one should wait with them until they were grown. And in the writings of Cyprian <note>Bishop of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD)</note>, the question first arose whether they should be baptized immediately after birth or on the 8th day. The adults were first well-instructed and mostly baptized in the days before Easter and Pentecost. *The same and the Council of Elvira.* <note>original: "Concilium Eliberitanum"; a Spanish synod held around 306 AD.</note>

<margin>The Lord’s Supper.</margin>§. 13. In the Lord’s Supper <note>original: "Abendmahl"</note>, many new ordinances were also added. Previously, it had been held in the evening and during a meal: now, it was performed early, and mostly on Saturdays and Sundays. <margin>Church discipline.</margin>
§. 15. In this and the previous time, the state of church discipline was as follows: among true Christians, there was initially no knowledge of banishment, violent expulsion, or condemnation. §. 16. But as many teachers began to rule over the congregations, another manner emerged in this regard, which we can see in the Church Councils. But not only was this often handled in a negligent and partisan way, it was also rarely orderly. ### 3rd Century. Chapter II. ###

<margin>Their Christianity.</margin>
<margin>J. C. <note>Likely an abbreviation for "Jesus Christ" or "Jesus's Christians."</note></margin>
The inner life of the Christians is quite recognizable. At least this common notion remains true: “As long as they were under **pressure and the cross** <note>A traditional metaphor for hardship and religious persecution.</note>, their **faith and love** certainly endured. §. 18. However, when weighed against the subsequent obvious decline, a **living faith** and many glorious fruits and gifts were still to be perceived among most, especially in the beginning. §. 19. Therefore, after him, **Anthony**, **Hilarion**, and many thousands of others served God in the greatest silence and earnest exercise of godliness. At the same time, among the other Christians, there were many **Ascetics** or those who, by abandoning all external things, practiced solely in the contemplation and performance of divine matters. *Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius, Basil the Great, Jerome, Socrates, Sozomen, Cassian.* <note>The author lists several prominent early church historians and theologians who wrote about the desert fathers and the rise of asceticism.</note>

Because of this, it has been said that he perished miserably in the battle against the Persians, and that he threw a handful of blood into the air and said: "You have conquered, O Galilean!" <note>original: "Du hast überwunden Galiläer!" This is the famous legendary phrase "Vicisti, Galilaee."</note> although the authors do not agree on this. The Pagans, on the other hand, said that a Christian had shot him, which the Christians did not exactly deny, and moreover defended and praised. *The Greeks according to Sozomen, Libanius, Sozomen, John of Damascus from Helladius.*

### On the internal condition of Christians.

<meta>catchword: times</meta>

<margin>Ceremonies.</margin>
§. 12. Thus, an incredible multitude of external ceremonies and ordinances came to light once people had turned away from true inward worship. The origin was mostly this: because many people, in order to please Emperor **Constantine**, declared themselves Christians, they mostly retained their old pagan habits and ceremonies, which could not easily be abolished because of the great number of people.

<margin>Superstition.</margin>
§. 13. At that time, pilgrimages to the tomb of Christ began, after **Constantine** and his mother <note>Empress Helena, who is traditionally credited with finding the "True Cross" in Jerusalem.</note> had built a church there and dedicated it with great splendor—an act that *Gregory of Nyssa* and others zealously spoke out against. Superstition regarding relics, the making of the sign of the cross, and the veneration of saints also emerged as people sought out the bodies of martyrs and interred them within the churches.

§. 14. People also began to build the most magnificent churches everywhere, in which they lit candles during the day, used incense, hung up images, and let everything depend upon external appearance. Added to this were the peculiar consecrations and the monuments to the martyrs, which were called <term>martyria</term> <note>original: "martyria"; structures built over the grave of a martyr or at a place of their suffering.</note> and <term>memories of the martyrs</term> <note>original: "memorias martyrum".</note>. The writers of this time are full of these and other things, especially the records of the church councils and the laws.

§. 15. New feast days were also added to those previously established.

## 4th Century. Chapter II.

<meta>catchword: in</meta>

<margin>Baptism.</margin>
§. 16. Very serious errors and abuses had crept into the practice of **baptism**. These included the fact that most people, and almost all of the most prominent ones, had themselves baptized only on their deathbeds. This is what **Constantine** and almost all the other Emperors did, under the delusion that they would thus be freed from all their sins at once. Indeed, sometimes they even baptized those who were already dead. *Eusebius, Socrates, Theodoret, Code of Canons of the African Church.*

<margin>The Lord's Supper.</margin>
§. 17. People also grew accustomed to receiving it only once a year, and otherwise did much that was contrary to its actual purpose. *Ambrose, Gregory Nazianzus, Council of Nicaea, Third Council of Carthage, Council of Alexandria according to Athanasius.*

### Chapter IV.
## Concerning the councils of this century.

-> §. 1. <-

<margin>The Nicene Council.</margin>
The most famous council in these times was the Nicene, the occasion of which was this: Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, had entered into a dispute with Arius, an elder <note>original: "Aeltisten," referring to a presbyter or priest.</note> there. During this, the former <note>Alexander</note> was more concerned with honor and made such propositions that appeared to Arius to be <margin>Arius's conflict.</margin> Sabellian <note>Sabellianism was a heresy which taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons, but merely different "modes" or masks of a single person.</note>, as the writers admit. Therefore, Arius argued against the equality of the Son with the Father as follows: “If the Father begat the Son, then the Son has a beginning of his being. Consequently, there was a time when the Son was not.” *Socrates Scholasticus, Sozomen, Theodoret, Epiphanius, Philostorgius.*

§. 2. Once this unfortunate dispute had begun with mere human reason and empty words, the parties soon split, and each side attracted its own following. The Bishop drove Arius and others out of the city. Constantine indeed sent Hosius <note>Hosius of Corduba, a trusted advisor to the Emperor.</note> there to reach a settlement; he disapproved of the entire dispute and considered it trivial and worthy of nothing. However, neither this nor other admonitions helped, so that he was finally persuaded by Alexander to call a council, with Alexander himself arranging everything. *The same authors and Eusebius.*

<margin>325 <note>The year 325 AD, the date of the Council of Nicaea.</note></margin>
<margin>Participants</margin>
§. 3. Thus, there gathered on the side of Alexander 318 bishops, not counting the other assistants, lesser church servants, and remaining people.

§. 9. ### 4th Century. Chapter IV.

...among whom there were only 17 Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being and not eternal with God the Father.</note>, and it is not known for certain whether Arius himself was present. ### On the Councils.

<margin>Other decrees.</margin>
§. 7. Following this, the time of Easter was also fixed to a specific day of the year, just as we still observe it today <note>Before this, different regions calculated Easter differently, with some following the Jewish Passover date.</note>. §. 8. Constantine now confirmed these and other conclusions, threatening all opponents with severe punishments. He ordered the books of the Arians <note>Followers of Arius who denied that Christ was fully divine and co-eternal with the Father.</note> to be burned and commanded that they be called "Porphyrians" <note>named after the pagan philosopher Porphyry, an enemy of Christianity; this was intended as a brand of shame.</note>, along with whatever other means of intimidation were used against them. Regarding the rulings of the bishops, he wrote in his decree that they should be held as highly as the words of Christ himself, because the Holy Spirit reveals God’s will to them. *Eusebius, letter in Gelasius, Socrates, Sulpicius Severus, etc.*

§. 9. However, all of this did not last long, as the Emperor soon thereafter became Arian himself, and the Arians took every measure against the Orthodox that the Orthodox had previously decreed against them. According to some reports, the synod lasted three years; according to others, only three months. *Cassiodorus, Cresconius’s Collection of Canons.*

Consequently, the clergy labeled these and others as heretics, a practice which later became even more common. *Notes on Augustine's "On Heresies."*

<header>### Concerning the Councils.</header>
<meta>catchword: §. 5.</meta>

...after the arrangement of Cyril of Alexandria, who intended to be the presiding officer <note>term: Praeses (Latin for "President" or "Presiding Officer")</note>, with the consent of Emperor Theodosius II; alongside him, 200 bishops and the delegates of the Roman Bishop <note>Referring to Pope Celestine I</note> were present.

§. 2. Nestorius did indeed arrive at Ephesus, but he refused to appear before the council because the Bishop of Antioch, John, had not yet arrived; John was reluctant to see Nestorius condemned. In the meantime, Cyril, along with others, nonetheless condemned Nestorius and deposed him from his bishopric <note>The Nestorian controversy centered on whether Mary could be called "Theotokos" (God-bearer). Nestorius preferred "Christotokos" (Christ-bearer), emphasizing the distinction between Christ's human and divine natures.</note>.

§. 3. However, because Nestorius had many patrons at the imperial court, the proceedings of the synod were poorly received. This resulted in Cyril being imprisoned along with Memnon, the Bishop of Ephesus, after John of Antioch and twenty-two others had condemned Cyril in their own separate assembly—an action the Emperor declared valid alongside the rejection of Nestorius. Finally, these two parties were barely reconciled with one <margin>at Antioch.</margin> another at a synod in Antioch. *Evagrius, Liberatus, Acts of the Synod of Ephesus.* <note>The author cites historical sources: Evagrius Scholasticus, the deacon Liberatus of Carthage, and the official records of the council.</note>

§. 4. At that same city of Ephesus, another synod was held regarding the case of Eutyches <note>Eutyches was a monk who argued that Christ had only one nature, a view known as Monophysitism</note>, which, however, was generally rejected and called λῃστρικὸν <margin>λῃστρικὸν</margin> <note>original: lēstrikon</note> or "murderous" <note>term: Robber Council (Latrocinium). This 449 AD council is historically infamous for the use of military force and intimidation to secure its theological decrees.</note>. Specifically, two synods had previously been held in Constantinople by Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian regarding this matter, in which Eutyches was rejected. He then aligned himself with Dioscorus, Bishop of Alexandria, who, through the influence of the court official Chrysaphius, brought about another synod.

### Of the Councils

§. 9. On the other hand, Nestorius, Eutyches, Dioscorus, and all their followers were condemned, specifically by the delegates of Leo <note>Pope Leo I, known as Leo the Great, whose "Tome" or letter laid the groundwork for the council's decisions</note>. These were held in the same esteem as the Holy Scriptures and the Gospels by Gregory the Great, Justinian, and others. *Evagrius, Liberatus, Leo the Great, Zonaras, Acts of the Council of Chalcedon.* <note>original: "Evagrius, Liberatus, Leo M. At the beginning of this century, the Pelagians became known in Britain, Italy, and Palestine. Their leader was named Pelagius, a Briton, and his followers were primarily Cœlestius and Julianus, along with others, against whom Augustine and Jerome wrote extensively.

And with this, the abomination fully and openly began with the <term>sacrifice of the Mass<note>original: "meß-opffer"; the theological concept that the priest offers Christ again during the service.</note></term> and all its abuses. *Life of Gregory the Great, Rabanus Maurus, Walafrid, Durandus, Polydore Vergil, Bona, etc.*

<margin>Benedict</margin>

<margin>540</margin>

§. 23. And all of this testifies clearly to the indescribable corruption of the Christians in this time. For their blindness in divine things is to be seen in their superstitious, miserable customs. Especially as they, instead of true worship, fell ever further into external ceremonies, as if they placed their highest duty toward God in these, and lost everything else because of them. From this came nothing but hypocrisy, false security <note>original: "sicherheit"; referring to a state of spiritual complacency or a false sense of salvation through rituals.</note>, malice, and the worst abominations, with which histories are filled and of which some <term>witnesses of the truth<note>original: "zeugen der wahrheit"; a term used by Protestant historians to identify individuals throughout history who supposedly maintained the "true" gospel against Roman Catholic errors.</note></term> write. *See the Catalog of the Witnesses of the Truth <note>original: "Catalogus Testium Veritatis"; a famous 1556 work by Matthias Flacius Illyricus listing historical opponents of the Papacy.</note>.*

<margin>Fifth Ecumenical Council. 553</margin>
**A**mong these, the most distinguished and famous is the so-called Fifth General Council, which was held in Constantinople at the instigation of the bishops and through the support of Justinian <note>Emperor Justinian I (reigned 527–565), known for his legal reforms and religious interventions.</note>. <margin>Origenists.</margin>
§. 2. The leader of these men, and also of the Acephali <note>original: "Acephalorum," meaning "the headless ones"; a sect of Monophysites who lacked a clear leader or "head."</note> (mentioned in the previous century), was Theodore, a superior of the monks in Caesarea.

And these were called the **Three Chapters** <note>original: "Tria Capitula"; a major theological dispute regarding these three specific sets of writings.</note>, which Justinian—at the suggestion of the aforementioned Theodore—condemned, specifically to please the Acephali.

# Concerning Heresies.
## D 5

<margin>Year of Christ</margin>
...the question was sharply disputed: Whether one could correctly say that one person of the Trinity was crucified? The Romans denied this, but the monks in Constantinople, and especially Maxentius <note>Johannes Maxentius, a leader of the so-called Scythian monks who promoted the formula "One of the Trinity suffered in the flesh."</note>, defended it; however, both sides probably did not know exactly what they were saying or asserting.

<margin>Dispute among the Orthodox.</margin>
§. 3. In addition to the sects mentioned above—the Arians, Nestorians, Eutychians, Armenians, etc.—the Acephali <note>original: "Acephalos," meaning "the headless ones," a term for various Monophysite groups who lacked a clear bishop or leader.</note> were now also called Severians after Severus, the Bishop of Antioch. He greatly oppressed the orthodox with his faction, but was later expelled and condemned again by Justin. *Evagrius, Liberatus.* <note>Historical sources: Evagrius Scholasticus and Liberatus of Carthage.</note>

<margin>536 Severians.</margin>
§. 4. These were also called Monophysites <note>original: "Monophysitas," meaning "those of one nature," who argued that Christ had a single, unified nature rather than distinct human and divine natures.</note>, because they acknowledged only one nature in Christ after his incarnation. Likewise, they were called Theopaschites <note>original: "Theopaschitas," from the Greek for "God-sufferers."</note>, because they taught that the divinity of the Son itself suffered and died after the flesh had been transformed into it.

<margin>Monophysites. Theopaschites.</margin>
§. 5. The Tritheists <note>original: "Tritheiten," those who viewed the Trinity as three separate divine beings.</note> followed John Philoponus and taught that the two natures <note>in Christ</note> were also two independent beings, and therefore there were also three such hypostases <note>original: "hypostases," a theological term for the distinct persons of the Trinity.</note> in God himself, which were entirely equal to one another. *Nicephorus, Suidas, Photius, Leontius Scholasticus.*

<margin>Tritheists.</margin>

# Chapter IV.
# On the Councils.

->§. 1.<-

<margin>608</margin>
<margin>General Councils. Third Council of Constantinople.</margin>
During this time, two so-called general councils were held in Constantinople, namely the Third Council of Constantinople—also known as the Sixth Ecumenical Council—and the Quinisextum.

<margin>Its causes.</margin>
§. 2. The former was assembled by Constantine IV against the Monothelites <note>A heretical group that believed Christ had two natures but only one "will" or operation</note>, after their leaders Cyrus and Sergius could not be suppressed by any other means, and many prominent bishops had defected to them, including Theodore, Bishop of Constantinople.

§. 3. For this purpose, Agatho of Rome sent four delegates, and the four Oriental Patriarchs came in person. These men, along with nearly 300 bishops, examined the writings of the Monothelites, confirmed the formulas of faith from the five previous general synods, and conversely condemned the Monothelites. Along with them, they condemned Pope Honorius, who had sided with the group. *Acts of the Sixth Synod.* <note>original: "Acta synodi VI."</note>

<margin>691</margin>
<margin>Quinisextum.</margin>
§. 4. The other general council was likewise assembled at Constantinople and was called *Quinisextum* <note>Latin for "Fifth-Sixth"</note>, because it was established to supplement the fifth and sixth synods, as no canons <term>ecclesiastical laws or rules</term> had been produced during them. It was also called *Trullanum*, however, because it took place in the *Trullo* (<term>τρούλλῳ</term> <note>original Greek: *troullō*</note>) or in a vaulted chamber of the imperial palace.

<margin>Monothelites.</margin>
Besides those who were already known previously—such as the Pelagians <note>Followers of Pelagius, who emphasized human free will over divine grace</note>, Nestorians <note>Followers of Nestorius, who emphasized the distinction between Christ’s human and divine natures</note>, Severians, Jacobites, Acephali <note>Literally "headless ones," a radical Miaphysite group</note>, Agnoetae <note>A sect that believed Christ’s human soul was limited in knowledge</note>, and so forth—only the Monothelites <term>A sect teaching that Christ had two natures but only one divine-human "will" (from the Greek *monos* "single" and *thelema* "will")</term> arose at this time; it was with them that the most disputes occurred.

<margin>630</margin>
<margin>Origin.</margin>
§. 2. These originated from the Eutychians <note>Followers of Eutyches, who argued Christ had a single nature where humanity was absorbed by divinity</note> and were especially nurtured by Cyrus, Bishop of Alexandria, and Sergius of Constantinople, as well as the following bishops of that city: Pyrrhus, Paul, Peter, Theoporius, and Marcian of Antioch, against whom the aforementioned council was also held.

<margin>Doctrines.</margin>
§. 3. They taught this: that in Christ there is only a single will and a single operation <note>referring to "energy" or activity</note>, namely that of the Divinity, which drives and governs the humanity. This opinion arose from a dispute among several teachers, after which everyone remained fixed in their own opinion—just as "word-wars" <term>bitter theological conflicts over precise terminology and definitions</term> were very common at that time.

<margin>Adherents.</margin>
§. 4. The Emperor himself and Pope Honorius I sided with these people, as the Pope's letter to Sergius demonstrates, though the Papists <note>A historical term used by the author to refer to Roman Catholic apologists</note> excuse him in vain. Because these powerful individuals were personally involved, a formula of faith was soon issued...

# The 8th Century.
### Chapter 1.
## Concerning the External State of the Church.

<meta>catchword: §. 9.</meta>

<margin>Leo III.</margin>

Nicephorus, Patriarch of Constantinople (not the one named Callistus <note>A reference to differentiate him from Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, a much later 14th-century historian.</note>) has left behind a *Historical Breviary* <note>original: "Breviarium historicum"; a concise history of the Byzantine Empire.</note> up to the year 769 AD; likewise, a chronological work up to the times of Michael and Theophilus.

<margin>Paul the Deacon.</margin>
§. 7. In the Latin church, there were almost even fewer famous people. Paul the Deacon <note>original: "Paulus Diaconus"; c. 720–799, a Benedictine monk and historian of the Lombards.</note> was first a deacon at Aquileia, afterwards the Chancellor to Desiderius, King of the Lombards, and finally a monk. He particularly described the history of the Lombards at great length up to the year 744, as well as the *Miscellaneous History* <note>original: "Historia Miscella"; an expansion of Eutropius's Roman history.</note> up to the 17th book (as many believe), to which the continuation from Theophanes was later added.
<margin>Miscellaneous History.</margin>

§. 8. Otherwise, it is also attributed to him that, by the command of Charlemagne <note>original: "Caroli M." (Carolus Magnus).</note>, he first arranged the *homiliarium* or the <term>Postils</term> <note>original: "postille"; a collection of sermons or commentaries on the Gospel readings used in the church year.</note> according to the Gospels. In history, he is very sincere and sensible, except that he greatly extols Gregory the Great <note>original: "Gregorium M." (Gregorius Magnus).</note> in his biography.
<margin>Postils.</margin>

<margin>Alcuin.</margin>
§. 9. Alcuin <note>original: "Alcuinus"</note>, also known as Flaccus Albinus, an Anglo-Saxon <note>original: "Engel-Sachse"</note> by birth and a student of Bede <note>original: "Bedæ"; St. Bede the Venerable.</note>, is said to have been the Preceptor <note>Tutor or chief advisor.</note> to Charlemagne and afterwards Abbot at Ferrara <note>Historically, Alcuin was the Abbot of St. Martin at Tours; "Ferrara" may be a transcription error in the original text or a confusion with Ferrières.</note>. He did not die until the following century, in 804, and wrote many interpretations of the Bible, as well as other treatises and letters, according to the understanding of his times.

### Chapter IV.
## Concerning the Councils.

->§. 1.<-

<margin>Ecumenical Councils. 4th Council of Constantinople.</margin>
During this time in the East, two Councils <note>original: "Synodi"</note> were held to be universal <note>original: "Oecumenicæ"; refers to councils whose decrees were meant to be binding for the whole Christian Church.</note>, yet they directly contradicted one another: namely, the 4th Council of Constantinople and the second Council of Nicaea. <margin>754 787</margin>

§. 2. The former is also called the 7th General Council by the Greeks and was assembled under Constantine Copronymus <note>Emperor Constantine V (reigned 741–775). The name "Copronymus" was a derogatory nickname given by his theological enemies.</note> from all the bishops of his empire, of whom there were nearly three hundred and fifty. However, the Pope did not attend because of his enmity toward the Emperor.

§. 3. The matter being handled was the dispute over images <note>The Iconoclastic Controversy, a period in Byzantine history when the use of religious images or icons was opposed by religious and imperial authorities.</note>, which shall be discussed further below. Regarding this, it was resolved that the first confessions of faith should stand, but all idolatry and the worship of images should be abolished from the churches, whether they might be <margin>Against the images.</margin>

# Concerning the Councils.

<margin>754 AD</margin> ...peror. <note>Continuing from the previous page: "the Emperor Constantine V."</note> This council prohibited any attempt to represent God, Christ, or the Saints through images.

<margin>The consequences of this.</margin> §. 4. Whereupon all images were removed, until Empress Irene and the Second Council of Nicaea <note>held in 787 AD</note> later reinstated them. However, the monks and others rebelled publicly against this removal, for which they were nonetheless punished; at the same time, the monastic system and the prohibition of marriage for priests were abolished. For this reason, the monks and the "friends of images" <note>iconodules</note> have incessantly slandered this Emperor and the Synod. *Theophanes, Acts of the Synod in the Acts of Nicaea II.*

<margin>787 AD</margin> <margin>Nicaea II, commonly called the False Nicaean Council <note>original: "Nicena II. vulgo Pseudo Nicena"; a term used by Western critics who did not recognize this council's authority.</note></margin> §. 5. The Second Council of Nicaea was held under the Empress Irene, who had pre-arranged the matter with Tarasius the Patriarch and Pope Hadrian. Indeed, they intended thereby to overturn the aforementioned Synod <note>of 754</note>, using all manner of cunning and force to do so, as Charlemagne <note>original: "Carolus M."</note> and others later complained.

§. 6. It was then resolved that the previous decrees <note>against images</note> were to be rejected as godless; conversely, all statutes concerning the worship of images <note>original: "bilder-dienst"</note> were confirmed, and this practice was to be established as holy and necessary. To this were added the most terrible curses and condemnations <note>anathemas</note> against those who spoke against it.

<margin>794 AD</margin> <margin>Council of Frankfurt.</margin> §. 7. In response to this, by the arrangement of Charlemagne, a Synod was held at Frankfurt am Main, consisting of 300 bishops from France, Germany, Spain, Italy, and England.

§. 8. Here, they first condemned the opinions of the Adoptianists <note>a heresy claiming Christ was only the "adopted" son of God in his human nature</note>, particularly those of Elipandus and Felix, of whom more will be said below.

### 8th Century. Chapter IV.

Furthermore, the aforementioned Council of Nicaea <note>the Second Council of Nicaea, 787 AD, which reinstated image worship</note> was rejected, and it was established instead that such worship of images must be avoided. In this context, the decree <note>original: "capitulare"</note> of Emperor Charlemagne <note>original: "Caroli"</note> against that council was confirmed. *Hincmar of Reims and the Acts according to Sirmond.*

<margin>Roman councils.</margin>
§. 9. Otherwise, many synods <note>church councils</note> were held in Italy, and in Rome all were held according to the will and advantage of the Popes. Among others, the Council of Friuli <note>original: "Forojulienfische," held in 796 or 797 AD</note> under Paulinus <note>Paulinus II of Aquileia</note> against Felix <note>Felix of Urgell, who promoted Adoptianism, the belief that Christ was the adopted son of God</note> is well known.
<margin>Friuli.</margin>

<margin>German councils.</margin>
§. 10. In Germany, under Carloman, King of the Franks, a council was held, the location of which is not named. Likewise, one was held at Lestines <note>original: "Liptinas," 743 AD</note> to improve church discipline <note>original: "kirchenzucht"</note>; however, this helped little, as one can see in the canons <note>church laws</note> of such councils the more than heathen abominations of the clergy and the common people.

§. 11. Following these, Charlemagne also arranged several councils at Aachen and Worms. Likewise, one at Regensburg, mostly to reform <note>original: "reformiren"</note> this or that in civil and church affairs.

<margin>French councils.</margin>
§. 12. In France, things were so miserable and sluggish under the rulers and teachers that even such outward customs fell behind, and almost no synod was held until the Council of Soissons <note>original: "Suessionenfische," 744 AD</note> under Pippin <note>Pippin the Short</note>. There, Clement the Scot and Aldebert were innocently condemned as heretics, though they were witnesses to the truth <note>these two figures are often viewed by later Protestant historians as early reformers who opposed the Roman Church's authority</note>.

§. 13. Afterwards came the Council of Ver <note>original: "Vernenfische," 755 AD</note> and then the Council of Gentilly <note>original: "Gentiliaca," 767 AD</note>, held under Pippin following the embassy of Emperor Constantine Copronymus <note>Constantine V; "Copronymus" was a derogatory nickname meaning "dung-named" given to him by his enemies who supported image worship</note>

<header>8th Century. Chapter V.</header>

...at the synods of Soissons and Mainz <note>The Council of Soissons (744) and Mainz (745) dealt largely with the reforms of Saint Boniface and the condemnation of his rivals</note>, they were condemned by the Pope. *Boniface and [Pope] Zachary in their letters. Aventinus. Bale.*

<margin>Iconoclasts. <term>Iconoclasts</term> <note>original: "Iconomachi"; literally "image-fighters"</note>. The origin of image worship.</margin>
§. 4. Thus, at the Roman synod, the <term>Iconoclasts</term> in the East were condemned as heretics, while among the Latins in the West, the worship of images was firmly established. For although images had been introduced into the churches almost as early as the 4th century for decoration and as memorials, it was in this century that people began to fall down before them, to pray to them, to offer incense, to light wax candles, and so forth.

<margin>And of image worship.</margin>
§. 5. Now, Emperor Philippicus and the Patriarch John rejected the 6th general council <note>The Third Council of Constantinople (680–681)</note> because they were <term>Monothelites</term> <note>a group believing Christ had only one will, rather than a divine and a human will</note>. For this reason, they removed the images from the Church of Saint Sophia <note>the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople</note> that depicted this council and had been placed there by Justinian.

§. 6. Whereupon the Pope took the opposite position and defended the custom of using images. In contrast, Leo III, the Emperor, zealously campaigned against them—for which reason they called him an Iconoclast <note>original: "Iconomachum"</note>—as did his son Constantine <note>Constantine V, often derisively called "Copronymus" by his enemies</note>. Consequently, both parties condemned one another at various synods and elsewhere. Under Empress Irene in the East, image worship was again strengthened. In the West, however, Charlemagne <note>original: "Carolo M."</note> only permitted their use <note>as educational tools or decorations</note>, but not their worship, which was contrary to the opinion of the Popes. See above in the first 3 councils and Theophanes. *Paul the Deacon, Anastasius, Zonaras, Kedrenos, Spanheim, History of Images.*

<margin>Dispute over the Holy Spirit.</margin>
§. 7. We heard in the previous century about the dispute between the Greeks and the Latins regarding the procession of the Holy Spirit <note>This refers to the *Filioque* controversy, a major cause of the eventual split between the Orthodox and Catholic churches, concerning whether the Holy Spirit comes from the Father alone or from both the Father and the Son</note>. This time, they contradicted one another at public synods, and the Greeks established at the Council of Nicaea <note>the Second Council of Nicaea, 787 AD</note>: **The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone.**

<margin>Jacobites.</margin>
§. 8. Likewise, at this time, the <term>Jacobites</term> <note>a Miaphysite Christian group in the Middle East and Egypt</note> became very strong in Egypt; they are called <term>Copts</term> or Coptics to this day after the city of Coptos, and they continue to endure.

<margin>Felicians. Adoptianists.</margin>
§. 9. In particular, much has been said and written in the West concerning the Felicians. These originated with Felix, Bishop of Urgell in the Pyrenees mountains, and with Elipandus, Bishop of Toledo.

<margin>Elipandus.</margin>
§. 10. They are said to teach: while Christ is indeed the true Son of God according to his divine nature, and therefore also true God; according to his humanity, however, he is an adopted son, and is God in name only. From this, they are called <term>Adoptianists</term> <note>original: "Adoptiani"</note>. Consequently, they were accused of establishing two sons in Christ and thus two persons, which would have made them <term>Nestorians</term> <note>followers of a 5th-century doctrine that emphasized the disunity of Christ’s human and divine natures</note>.

§. 11. Because of this, they were condemned by the Pope and the synods of Friuli, Regensburg, and Frankfurt, and elsewhere by various bishops. Although they also had many followers, as both Felix and Elipandus were very popular due to their scholarship and piety. *Eginhardus, Agobardus, Alcuin, Annals of Fulda.* <note>These are historical sources: Einhard was Charlemagne's biographer; Agobard was Archbishop of Lyon; Alcuin (Alaninus) was a leading scholar of the Carolingian Renaissance; and the Annals of Fulda are a major record of East Frankish history.</note>

### Ninth Century. Chapter IV.
<header>Ninth Century. Chapter IV.</header>
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

<margin>First Council of Constantinople <note>original Latin: "Constantinopolitanum I"</note></margin>
§. 2. The first council was convened by Emperor **Michael** <note>Michael III, r. 842–867</note> and consisted of 318 bishops; it was held partly because of the controversy over religious images <note>The second phase of Byzantine Iconoclasm</note>, and partly against Patriarch Ignatius, who was deposed and replaced by Photius. *Balsamon, Zonaras, Alexius, Aristenus.* <note>These are prominent medieval commentators on canon law.</note> <margin>861</margin>

<margin>II</margin>
§. 3. The second council was held by Basil the Macedonian <note>Basil I</note> against Photius and in favor of Ignatius, an action which the Roman Popes also approved. However, matters there proceeded in a very frivolous and violent manner, as Nicetas himself confesses. For this reason, most people have rejected this <term>synod <note>A council of church leaders convened to decide on doctrine or discipline.</note></term>. <margin>869</margin>

<margin>III</margin>
§. 4. The third council was held by this same Emperor on behalf of Photius, whom he reinstated. This synod is regarded as the eighth general <note>ecumenical</note> council, although the Roman side is not entirely satisfied with it. <margin>879</margin>

§. 5. In the <term>Occident <note>The West; specifically Western Europe.</note></term>, almost countless synods were held, though none occurred in Spain, because the Saracens <note>The Muslim rulers of Al-Andalus</note> had suppressed everything there.

<margin>Mainz <note>original Latin: "Moguntinum"</note></margin>
§. 6. <margin>Valence <note>original Latin: "Valentinum"</note></margin>
<margin>855</margin>

<margin>Tribur <note>original Latin: "Triburiense"</note></margin>

## Chapter V.
## Concerning the Controversies.

->§. 1.<-

<margin>Dispute over the Lord’s Supper <note>original: "Abendmahl"</note>.</margin>
From the conflict over religious images <note>The Iconoclast Controversy, discussed in the previous century</note>, another dispute arose concerning the Lord’s Supper. This occurred because those who rejected the images argued that the Lord’s Supper was the only true and living image of Christ; however, others denied this and sought the actual body of Christ within the sacrament itself.

<margin>820</margin>
§. 2. In the Latin Church, a monk named Paschasius Ratbertus wrote a book about the body and blood of Christ, claiming that the bread and wine are transformed into the true flesh and blood of Christ and that all communicants receive them. <margin>Transubstantiation.</margin> With this, he laid the foundation for the Papal doctrine of <term>Transubstantiation <note>The theological doctrine that the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the substance of the Body and Blood of Christ during the Eucharist.</note></term>.

§. 3. Conversely, Bertramus (also known as Ratramnus), John Scotus <note>Johannes Scotus Eriugena</note>, and others contradicted him, stating that Christ's body was present in a natural, spiritual manner, but not literally <note>original: "wahrhafftig," truly or actually</note> within the bread. This opinion, however, was later condemned in the 9th century, while the former was accepted, as men fought over opinions and forgot what was more necessary.

<margin>Concerning Divine Election <note>original: "Gnadenwahl"</note>, Gottschalk.</margin>
§. 4. Another and sharper dispute arose from a Benedictine monk named Gottschalk <note>original: "Godefchalcus"</note>, who brought forward again the doctrine of divine election <note>The concept of Predestination</note>, which had been recounted at the end of the 5th century.

<margin>Predestinarians <note>original Latin: "Prædestinatiani"</note>.</margin>
§. 5. Against him now fought Hincmar of Rheims in his own writings, and Rabanus <note>Hrabanus Maurus</note> in Mainz <note>original: "Mäyntz"</note>

<summary>This page describes the emergence of two major theological conflicts in the 9th-century Latin Church: the debate over the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist (leading toward the doctrine of Transubstantiation) and the revival of the controversy over Predestination by the monk Gottschalk.</summary>

<margin>Idolatry. Relics.</margin>
§. 13. Even the greatest and otherwise clever rulers were completely submerged in the idolatry of relics and sacred objects. ### Chapter V.
## On Religious Disputes.

->§. 1.<-

The schisms between the Roman and Greek churches mentioned in the previous century were continued and increased even further during this time. One party constantly condemned the teachings, customs, and followers of the other. *See Photius’s Encyclical Letter.* <note>original: *Vid. §. 2. Apart from these and the previously mentioned new opinions, the writers of this period record no other heresies. For the rest, the fundamental errors of the papal religion were increasingly accumulated, introduced, and spread.

Martin II <note>likely referring to Pope Martin IV, who reigned in the late 13th century and granted these privileges</note> gave the Order of Preachers and the Minorites the privilege to hear confessions and hold Mass.
