<margin>Auricular confession. Transubstantiation. The cup in the Lord's Supper.</margin>
§. 16. <term>Auricular confession</term> <note>the practice of confessing sins privately to a priest</note> was now, in <margin>1225</margin>, so firmly established by Pope Innocent III at the Lateran Council that it was claimed no one could be saved without it. At the same time, **Transubstantiation** <note>the doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the actual substance of the body and blood of Christ</note> was confirmed, and the cup in the Lord's Supper was taken away from the <term>laity</term> <note>the "common people" of the church, as opposed to the ordained clergy</note>. *Bale, Mornay, Daillé.*

<margin>Jubilee.</margin>
§. 17. Boniface VIII established the **Jubilee** for every hundred years, in order to gain money and otherwise keep the people in constraint and obedience. *Platina, Krantz, Bale, Nauclerus.*

### Of the internal condition of the Churches.

X 2
<meta>catchword: over</meta>

Regarding the previous abundance <note>referring to the many innovations mentioned on the previous page</note> of such things, there is almost nothing left to add. However, John XXII devised the rule that the bells should be rung three times a day, and <margin>Bell ringing.</margin> during this, the *Hail Mary* <note>original: "ave Maria"</note> should be prayed. *Polydorus Virgilius.* <note>Polydore Vergil (c. 1470–1555), an Italian historian active in England.</note>

<margin>Judgment of foreigners.</margin> §. 7. The Papal abominations were so loathsome even to the most distant peoples that the Greeks, when this Pope exhorted them to be obedient to him, answered him thus: "We believe your power over your subjects well enough, but we cannot endure your pride, and we cannot satisfy your greed. Satan is with you, and the Lord is with us!" *Joh. de Mondevilla.* <note>Sir John Mandeville, the purported author of a famous 14th-century travel memoir.</note>

<margin>Pride and greed of the clergy.</margin> §. 8. Among the rest of the clergy, greed and ambition were so great that even the Popes themselves were forced to publish bulls <note>official papal edicts</note> against them (*as cited in Bzovius*), and by the visual splendor of their clothing, one could no longer distinguish the so-called clergy from the worldly. Because of this, the Bishops and the Canons at Constance <note>original: "Costnitz"</note> once fought violently amongst one another. *Frossardus, Felix Faber.*

§. 9. ## Chapter IV.
## On the Councils.

->§. 1.<-

<margin>1414</margin><margin>Constance.</margin><margin>Its proceedings.</margin>The most famous among these is the Council of Constance in Swabia, which was assembled through the efforts of Sigismund <note>Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund</note> by Germans, French, Spanish, Italians, and English. At first, action was taken against John XXIII <note>An "Antipope" deposed by the council to end the Papal Schism</note>, of which we spoke above in Chapter 1.

§. 2. To this place also came Jan Hus and Jerome of Prague with an Imperial safe-conduct <note>A document guaranteeing their safety</note>, but as they would not recant, they were burned there—the latter one year after the former. Following this, their teachings were further condemned along with those of Wycliffe, and it was decided to give the Lord's Supper to the laity only in one form, or as bread alone, with the words: *notwithstanding the act of Christ* <note>original Latin: "non obstante facto Christi"</note>. This means: even though Christ had handled it differently <note>The Council acknowledged that Christ offered both bread and wine, but decreed that the Church could restrict the wine to priests only</note>.

<margin>Conclusion.</margin>§. 3. Otherwise, much concerning a reformation was brought to the table, but nothing reached a conclusion or effect, and the Council was dissolved after four years in the 45th session. *Aeneas Sylvius, Platina, Theobaldus, History of the Councils as now edited by Hermann von der Hardt.*

## Chapter IV.
# Of the Councils.

->§. 1.<-

<margin>1414</margin><margin>Constance.</margin><margin>Its proceedings.</margin>The most famous among these is the Council of Constance <note>original: "Concilia Costnitz"</note> in Swabia, which was assembled through the efforts of Sigismund <note>Sigismund of Luxembourg, Holy Roman Emperor</note> by Germans, French, Spanish, Italians, and English. At that time, proceedings were first held against John XXIII <note>Referencing the Pisan Pope Baldassare Cossa, who was deposed during the Great Schism</note>, of which we spoke above in Chapter 1.

§. 2. To this place also came Jan Hus and Jerome of Prague with an Imperial safe-conduct <note>A document ensuring protection for a traveler, which the Council ultimately ignored</note>, but since they would not recant, they were burned there, the latter one year after the former. Following this, their teachings—alongside those of Wycliffe—were further condemned, and it was decreed that the Lord's Supper should be given to the laity <term>laity: members of the church who are not ordained clergy</term> only under one form <note>Giving only the bread and withholding the wine from the congregation</note>, or in the bread alone, with these words: *non obstante facto Christi.* That is: notwithstanding the fact that Christ had acted otherwise <note>original: "non obstante facto Christi. Das ist: ob es schon Christus anders gehandelt hätte." This controversial decree acknowledged that Christ instituted the sacrament in both kinds (bread and wine) but asserted the Church's authority to restrict the cup.</note>.

<margin>Outcome.</margin>§. 3. Otherwise, much regarding a reformation was indeed brought to the table <note>original: "aufs tapet gebracht"</note>, but nothing came to a conclusion or effect, and the Council was dissolved after four years in its 45th session. *Aeneas Sylvius, Platina, Theobaldus, History of the Councils as now edited by Hermann von der Hardt.* <note>These refer to Renaissance and early modern historians who documented the Council's proceedings.</note>

And at Torgau, a convention was held concerning the Sacrament controversy <note>This refers to the ongoing dispute over the "Real Presence" of Christ in the Eucharist, a major dividing line between Lutherans and the Reformed.</note>, in order to restrain the Reformed, who were removed from the Electorate of Saxony.

<margin>Formula of Concord. 1577.</margin>
§. 15. On the other hand, the Formula of Concord <note>original: "Formula Concordiæ." This document was intended to settle various Lutheran controversies and remains a foundational statement of Lutheran belief.</note> was produced at Torgau, and later in the Bergen Monastery near Magdeburg, by Jacobus Andreæ, Musculus, Cörner, Selneccer, Chemnitius, and Chytræus. This was finally published after much dispute and opposition from others abroad.

<margin>Calendar Dispute. 1582.</margin>
§. 16. After this, the dispute over the new calendar began, which Pope Gregory XIII wished to impose upon the Protestants <note>The Gregorian calendar was introduced by the Pope in 1582; many Protestants initially resisted it as a "papist" imposition, preferring to keep the old Julian calendar.</note>. Furthermore, a dispute arose over exorcism in baptism in the Electorate of Saxony, where the Reformed and others rejected it, and many writings were exchanged regarding it; also many were driven out and deposed, and specifically in Anhalt there was great unrest over it.
<margin>Exorcism. 1591. 1596.</margin>

<margin>Huber. 1592.</margin>
§. 17. Samuel Huber, a professor at Wittenberg, contended with the theologians Polycarpus Lyser, Hunnius, Gesner, and others, arguing that there was a universal election by God <note>The "Huberian Controversy" centered on Huber's view that God had elected all people to salvation, which his colleagues viewed as a dangerous departure from the doctrine of predestination.</note>, about which there was much dispute.

## Chapter IV.
## Regarding the Councils and Colloquies.

->§. 1.<-

<margin>Councils.</margin>The Catholics <note>original: "Papisten"; a term used in this period by Protestant writers to refer to supporters of the Papacy.</note> organized several councils at this time to maintain themselves and their affairs. The first, however, was held by the Cardinals alone against Pope Julius III; it was held first <margin>Council of Pisa.</margin>at Pisa, then in Milan, and finally in Lyon.

§. 2. In response, the Pope held one himself, the 5th <margin>Lateran Council.</margin>Lateran Council in Rome, where across 15 sessions <note>original: "sessionibus"</note> nothing regarding the faith was confirmed except for the immortality of the soul. Furthermore, it was claimed that certain abuses in the churches and schools were to be improved, though this did not achieve much.

§. 3. Particularly famous is the Council of <margin>Council of Trent.</margin>Trent <note>original: "Tridentinum"</note>, which lasted for 18 years and was interrupted several times. In attendance were the Cardinals and the Pope's Legates, 4 Archbishops, and 35 Bishops, along with 47 Doctors of Theology.

§. 4. The proceedings <note>original: "tractaten"</note> themselves moved forward very slowly; in the first three sessions, almost nothing of consequence was undertaken, and in the remaining 22 sessions, the Papal tenets were repeated one after another, while the opposing views <note>referring to the Protestant arguments</note> were condemned. <header>16th Century. Chapter IV.</header>

<margin>Worms.</margin>
Johannes Brenz, Jakob Runge, and Johannes Pistorius met once more in Worms to discuss the "rule of faith" <note>the standard or authority used to settle doctrinal disagreements</note> in the religious dispute. However, they soon parted ways.

<margin>Heidelberg. 1560</margin>
§. 11. In Heidelberg, the Lutherans Joachim Mörlin and Johannes Stössel conferred with the Reformed theologians regarding the Lord’s Supper, though once again it was in vain.

<margin>Weimar. 1560</margin>
§. 12. In Weimar, Matthias Flacius and Victorinus Strigel disputed with one another regarding original sin. This led to a great schism, and Strigel also came into conflict with others regarding <term>Synergism</term> <note>the doctrine that the human will cooperates with divine grace in the process of conversion</note>.

<margin>Poissy <note>original: "Possiaci"</note>. 1561</margin>
§. 13. In France, King Charles IX arranged a <term>Colloquy</term> <note>a formal theological discussion or conference</note> between the Catholic and Reformed theologians—including Theodore Beza, Peter Martyr Vermigli, and Augustin Marlorat—specifically regarding the Lord’s Supper, but it bore no fruit.

<margin>1564</margin>
§. 14. At Maulbrunn, in the presence of Elector Frederick of the Palatinate and Duke Christoph of Württemberg, the Heidelberg theologians disputed with those from Württemberg. There, the Lord’s Supper, the presence of Christ, and His humanity were discussed without success, as neither party was willing to yield.

<margin>Altenburg. 1568</margin>
§. 15. In Altenburg, the Meissen theologians <note>the "Philippists," followers of Melanchthon</note> argued very heatedly with the Thuringian theologians <note>the "Gnesio-Lutherans," or "genuine" Lutherans</note> regarding <term>adiaphora</term> <note>matters of religious practice deemed "indifferent" because they are neither commanded nor forbidden by Scripture</note>, justification, and free will. This was conducted entirely in writing. Because of this, the dispute lasted nearly half a year, until they finally departed from one another with much resentment; subsequently, many in Thuringia were deposed from their offices and driven out.

They also began to persecute the <margin>Persecution of the Huguenots.</margin> Huguenots <note>French Protestants who followed the teachings of John Calvin</note> in France, and by all kinds of torments forced them to renounce their faith. Finally, in <margin>1685</margin> they completely overturned the Edict of Nantes <note>a decree from 1598 that had granted French Protestants substantial rights; its revocation led to mass exodus</note>, which had remained since the time of Henry II <note>original: "Henrico II"; likely a clerical error for Henry IV, who originally issued the Edict</note>. Consequently, countless Reformed people fled to Holland and Germany after everything had been taken from them.

§. 22. In England, there was much unrest under James II <margin>James II.</margin> <note>original: "Jacobo II"</note>, partly because of the Duke of <margin>1678</margin> Monmouth, whom he had beheaded; and partly because of the King's conversion to the Papacy <note>Catholicism</note> and the introduction of Papists into the realm. Therefore, in <margin>1689</margin> his son-in-law William, Prince of Orange <margin>William.</margin>, came to the aid of the Protestants and brought the designs of the Papists to nothing <note>referring to the Glorious Revolution</note>.

<margin>Disputes among the Papists <note>a historical term for Catholics</note>.</margin>
§. 2. Among these popes, the following remarkable things occurred within the Roman Church. The Jesuits <note>the Society of Jesus</note> and the Dominicans <note>the Order of Preachers</note> disputed sharply against one another under Paul V regarding the points of grace and free will. Furthermore, Gregory XV eventually had to completely forbid the numerous disputes concerning the Immaculate Conception of Mary <note>the doctrine that the Virgin Mary was kept free of original sin from her own conception</note>.

He taught that grace works so powerfully that one cannot resist it, and that it is not universal, occurring only according to the preceding will of God. <margin>1638</margin>

<margin>His conflict.</margin>
§. 4. All of this was rejected by the Pope, but the theologians in Paris conversely called the Pope's infallibility into doubt. They fought against the Jesuits to such an extent that they even labeled them as heretics in a book. <margin>1644</margin>

<margin>M. Antonius de Dominis.</margin>

For this reason, he was left to die in prison, and Urban VIII had his body burned <note>de Dominis was an Archbishop who defected to Anglicanism but later returned to Rome, where he was declared a heretic</note>.

This was the source of a large part of the unrest mentioned above <note>referring to the English Civil War</note>.

### XVII Century. Chapter II.

<margin>Attempted Unity.</margin>
§. 9. Meanwhile, the Reformed <note>also known as Calvinists</note> often sought to become one with the Lutherans. Regarding this, the writings of Dury <note>John Dury (Duræus), a Scotsman who worked tirelessly for Protestant union</note>, Alting, Pareus, and Bergius are available, as are the opposing writings of Weller, Hülsemann, Calov, and others. Among the Reformed themselves, Hugo Grotius <note>a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note> was rejected by Rivet and others, just as Calixtus and the theologians from Helmstedt and Königsberg were turned away by the Lutherans because of the reconciliation they sought.

<margin>Arminians. Gomarists. Synod of Dordrecht.</margin>
§. 10. Prior to this, a conflict occurred among the Reformed in Holland with the Arminians, who were also called Remonstrants <note>from their 1610 "Remonstrance" or protest against certain Calvinist doctrines</note>, while their opponents were called Gomarists after Franciscus Gomarus. The former wished to somewhat soften the harsh opinions of Calvin and Beza <note>referring to the strict doctrine of predestination</note>, which led to all manner of disputes until they were condemned by the Synod of Dordrecht <note>original: "Synodus zu Dordrecht," held in 1618–1619 to settle the controversy</note>. <margin>1610</margin>

<margin>Amyraut. Nonconformists. Separatists. Brownists. Independents.</margin>
§. 11. Following this, a dispute arose between Moïse Amyraut <note>original: "Mose Amyraldo," a French theologian who proposed "hypothetical universalism"</note>, Moulin, and others. In England, the Nonconformists separated from the Separatists and the Brownists <note>early English dissenters from the Church of England</note>, particularly after the beheading of King Charles <note>Charles I, executed in 1649</note> when the bishops and the liturgy were abolished. On the other hand, some refused to submit to the government of the church ministers; these were called Independents.

<margin>Quakers.</margin>
§. 12. During this time, the people known as Quakers became particularly well known, along with many other sects, of which about forty were counted in England at that time. <margin>1650</margin> In Holland, however, the theologians argued fiercely against the new philosophy of Descartes <note>original: "Cartesius"</note>, so much so that it was eventually banned. <margin>1650</margin>
<margin>Descartes.</margin>
